correctness.rationale: In each odd prime-power factor the only nonconstant coordinates have unit shifts, and they leave baseline 1 on their respective mod-p classes. At 2 the even shifts stay at 1, the odd shifts have baseline 2, and departures are possible only when the exponent is at least 2, on their respective mod-4 classes. With distinct classes at most one coordinate departs, so for disjoint groups the nonnegative increments of arbitrary increasing observables have zero product. CRT gives independent factors. Conditioning on one block gives nonpositive conditional covariance within the other block and nonpositive covariance of the increasing conditional means; induction and products on disjoint prime-coordinate sets give the full divisor-order assertion. On a collision the two threshold indicators coincide and have positive variance (probability 1/(p-1) at odd p and 1/2 at 4), proving necessity on pairs. At n=1 and on a sole factor 2 all coordinates are constant. For unit opposite shifts the local mean e+1 follows by summing phi(p^j) times the probability of a congruence mod p^j. At odd primes at least one local gcd equals 1; at 2 at least one equals 2. These identities give the stated mixed means and strict covariance except at n=1,2.

Bounded corroboration, not the general proof.

originality.rationale: The supported distinct contribution is the sharp classification of full divisor-order negative association for a common uniform unit, including its pairwise equivalence. Neither the inspected arithmetic moment and simultaneous-count results nor the classical general closure argument supplies that classification. No novelty is attributed to the opposite-shift mean, individual covariance formulas, or negative association closure.

value.rationale: For a common sample of a standard arithmetic quantity the classification replaces exponentially many group monotonicity tests by simple congruence checks. It identifies the nontrivial 2-adic boundary (parity alone is insufficient) and explains precisely why checking pairs suffices in this family, rather than just giving a known average.
